heading: One name, eight generations, four languages
lead: Every clerk who ever wrote this family down wrote its commonest given name in his own language. **Joannes in the church books, Zuane in Venetian, Giovanni in Italian, Ivan in Croatian, John in the diaspora** — and the archive counts **twenty-nine distinct written forms** of it. What follows is not the twenty-nine. It is the one name coming down this line, generation by generation, in the exact form the record uses — including the two generations where it disappears, and the one where it comes back.

rows.note: The earliest man of the name this archive can put on the road. A **Zuane** De Franceschi of Mione is on the headmen's list of the County of Pazin, with his son. *Zuane* is what Venice called John.
The first generation of the spine. The parish clerk writes him in Latin, because the church wrote in Latin; his neighbours would have called him **Giovanni**.

Farmer of house 5, Gračišće. The register abbreviates him the way it abbreviates everyone — **Joan. Bapt.** — and the same three generations of clerks would have said *Giobatta*. He lived under three sovereignties without moving house.

**Here the name goes underground.** He is Antonio, not Giovanni — but the register will not let his father go: *q. Joannis*, **son of the late Giovanni**. Three Latin words, and they are what tie house 19 to house 5 and carry this whole descent. The name survives one generation as a piece of grammar.

rows.lang: Latin in church, Croatian in life
rows.who: Josip Defranceschi, stonemason then factory hand
rows.note: Gone. He is Joseph, and the register writes **Josephus** while the coast around him is already saying **Josip**. He is also the man who takes the family down from the county to the sea — and the first of the line whose name is written in Croatian by people who are not clerks.

Still gone, and now the surname changes instead: **Defranceski**, fused and without the -sch, is the spelling that reaches the twentieth century. He was baptised under Austria, made an Italian subject at Rapallo without moving, and died under occupation.

**And here it comes back.** After two generations underground the name returns in its Croatian form. He went to work at Reutlingen at sixteen in October 1941 — and the German papers, which Germanised a great deal, left him **Ivan**. Not Johann. The clerks of the Reich wrote the Croatian form.
Twice in a row, deliberately. A name only repeats like this when a family means it to.

The name comes out the far end as a **middle name in English** — which is what happens to a given name when a family crosses a language and wants to keep something. It has now been **Zuane, Joannes, Giovanni, Giobatta, Josip's brother's, Ivan and Ivan again**, and it is still here.

close: Read down the column and the shape is plain. **The name is present for three generations, survives one more only as a patronymic, vanishes for two, and returns for three.** That is not carelessness. It is what a family name does when the language of the clerks changes four times in two hundred years — and the moment it comes back, in 1925, is the moment the family starts writing itself in Croatian rather than being written down in someone else's language.
formsnote: The twenty-nine forms of this one name that appear somewhere in this archive's records. Latin, Venetian, Italian, Croatian, German, English, French, Spanish — the same man, in whichever language the pen belonged to.
source_on: The generations are the Direct Line page, built from the Gračišće Status Animarum of 1870 and 1925, the Klenovica and Crikvenica registers, and the Pfullingen and Reutlingen labour papers. The name forms are this archive's own index of given names across every record it holds.
